title: One line of text that can break a login page
description: SQL injection happens when a website mixes your typing into its database commands. Parameterised queries stop it by keeping data and code apart.

scenes.big: One line can break a login
scenes.say: One line typed into a login box can trick a website into handing over its database. This is SQL injection.

scenes.caption: A login box, tricked
scenes.say: Here's the classic textbook example. The site glues your typing into its database question. Add an apostrophe, then OR one equals one, and the question becomes: is the name blank, or is one equal to one? That's always true.

scenes.sub: the bug: input read as instructions
scenes.say: The flaw is simple. The database can't tell your data from the developer's instructions, because they arrive mixed together in one string.
The fix is parameterised queries. The developer sends the query shape first, with blanks in it. Your input is sent separately, and the database only ever treats it as data, never as code.

steps: Validate input as a second layer
scenes.say: So: parameterise every query, validate input as a backup, and give the database account only the permissions it needs. Follow, and I'll unpack another threat next.
